deep.reconstruction:
The page has no text or formulas. It holds one pencil drawing, so the reading below is an interpretation, not a derivation.

(1) What is drawn. The whole sheet carries a regular square array of dots. This is a lattice, which I read as the Gaussian integers a+bi plotted in the plane. Over part of it Gauss drew a second, tilted square grid. Its sides are not parallel to the dot lattice; they run at roughly 20-30 degrees to the horizontal. A tilted square sublattice of Z^2 is exactly the set of multiples m·Z[i] of a Gaussian integer m = a+bi with a, b ≠ 0. Each tilted cell is then a fundamental domain, i.e. a complete residue system modulo m, holding N(m) = a^2+b^2 lattice points. The grid is clipped by an irregular convex polygon, about 9-10 cells across.

(2) The labels. Inside the polygon the lattice points carry one of: a digit 0, 1, 2 or 3; a cross ×; or a plain dot ·. The digits 0-3 are, almost certainly, exponents k of the unit i^k (my interpretation). This is the standard bookkeeping of Gauss's biquadratic-residue theory (Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum, Commentatio prima 1828, secunda 1832). There, for a Gaussian prime modulus m, every residue z not divisible by m has a quartic character [z/m] = i^k, with z^{(N(m)-1)/4} ≡ i^k (mod m). The crosses and dots would then mark a further class. Plausible candidates are: points ≡ 0 mod m or lying on the cell boundaries (multiples of m); points not divisible by 1+i; or simply unlabelled lattice points.

(3) Alternative reading. The labels may instead record a geometric 'Gauss lemma'. Here each product z·r is reduced into a central square, and one records which of the four quadrants (index k, rotation by i^k) it falls into. Gauss used this representation of complex residue systems by squares in the plane in Commentatio secunda.

(4) Whichever of these readings is right, the purpose is the same: a visual tabulation of residue classes of Gaussian integers modulo a Gaussian modulus, labelled by powers of i. That is, empirical material for the theory of biquadratic residues.

I cannot reliably read the label pattern from the image. It is therefore impossible to say whether the labels repeat with the period of the tilted grid, which would identify m (for example 2+i with N=5, or 3+2i with N=13). This is why I propose no specific computation as 'Gauss's'. The checks listed below verify only the arithmetic facts any such table must obey.
errors: No computational claims can be checked against the drawing itself. The label positions in the transcription are too uncertain to verify that the pattern is periodic modulo a single Gaussian integer. In a few places the visible labels seem to put a cross at several consecutive points along a lattice diagonal, which would be inconsistent with '× = multiples of m'. This could be my misreading of positions rather than a slip by Gauss.

results.what: Picture of a square-lattice tiling of Z[i] by the multiples of a Gaussian integer m (complete residue systems as tilted squares), with lattice points labelled by exponents 0-3 of powers of i and by special marks
results.modern_name: Geometric representation of Z[i]/(m) by a fundamental domain of the ideal lattice; quartic (biquadratic) residue character / unit classes
results.usually_credited_to: C. F. Gauss, Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum (1828, 1832); later geometric lattice-point proofs of reciprocity by Eisenstein (1844)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a working sketch tabulating residues of Gaussian integers on a tilted lattice. That geometric viewpoint is documented in Gauss's published second memoir on biquadratic residues (1832) and in his Nachlass. Nothing beyond known Gaussian material can be read off the page.

checkable.asserts: Modulo the Gaussian prime 3+2i (norm 13), i corresponds to 5 in F_13.
5^2 ≡ -1 mod 13, consistent with i^2 = -1 in Z[i]/(3+2i).
In Z[i]/(2+i) ≅ F_5 with i ≡ 3: 1 ≡ i^0, 3 ≡ i^1, 4 ≡ i^2, 2 ≡ i^3. So each nonzero class gets a unique label k in {0,1,2,3}, the quartic character z^((5-1)/4) = z.
Lists the quartic characters z^3 mod 13 for the residues modulo 3+2i. Each value in {1,5,12,8} (= i^0, i^1, i^2, i^3) occurs exactly 3 times.
3+2i ≡ 1 mod 2+2i, i.e. 3+2i is primary in Gauss's sense.

transcription_corrections: The page contains no text. The row-by-row label list in the machine transcription does not follow actual lattice rows; the labels sit on the points of the untilted dot lattice, not in rows of the tilted grid.
The dot lattice covers the whole lower half of the sheet outside the polygon, not only the interior.

Several cell-boundary lines are retraced more heavily, forming a staircase-like path through the grid in the lower part. This may mark a region boundary, such as a half- or quarter-system of residues, and is not recorded in the transcription.
The stamp 'Niedersächs. Staats- u. Univ.-Bibliothek Göttingen' appears in mirror image, showing through from the recto; it is not part of this page's content.
